Six traits, no simple candidate formula. 2026 House: separate lean-adjusted associations, not causal effects. Incumbency compares nominees; the
other five comparisons cover verified D incumbents. All six comparisons adjust for district presidential lean and lean squared; incumbency also adjusts for Republican incumbency. Party defection uses pre-election 119th-Congress party-dividing votes; ideology uses 2023-2024 votes. Intervals are twice their vote-share-scale values, with full-rank deletion and sample/leverage gates. 0 of six primary tests clear Holm p<0.05. Pointwise intervals are not multiple-comparison-adjusted. New descriptive biographies are not promoted into these models.

charts.alt:
Do candidate traits improve predictions?. 2026 House: change in state-and-person-held-out mean absolute error. Each pair uses identical people;
different rows cover different populations. These eight exploratory comparisons test added predictive information, not causal effects or forward forecast skill. Every comparison uses the same training and test people for its baseline and augmented model. Both models adjust for district lean and lean squared; both donor models also control known D/R incumbency. Individual record traits and their joint block apply only to verified Democratic incumbents. Cohorts differ across rows, so this is not a ranking of interchangeable candidate types. Intervals use a full-pipeline state jackknife, t(G-1) and complete-fold support gates; they are not multiple-comparison-adjusted.

charts.alt:
Start with the seat, not the candidate. 2026 House Democratic vote share versus the district's 2024 presidential share. Each dot is one
qualified contest; the diagonal marks equal shares. The diagonal is a descriptive equal-share reference, not an expected generic candidate, election forecast, national-wave adjustment or causal candidate effect. House geography uses the 2026 congressional map. All 435 House contests, including 30 held comparisons, remain in the complete queries. The all-candidate inventory also retains same-party candidates and noncandidate aggregate vote choices.

charts.alt:
Donor ideology gives a selected-sample answer. 2026 Democratic House candidates: a 0.5-point more conservative historical donor score. These scores
describe funding coalitions, not campaign platforms. Every row is a separately fitted observational association. Exact FEC/state/party matches with consistent names qualify. All name discrepancies are excluded here, including four aliases corroborated in a separate identity review. The nonincumbent group is below the 30-person publication gate; its diagnostic estimate and interval are retained in the CSV, not drawn as supported evidence. Models use known incumbency for both parties. No inference extends to all challengers, and the intervals are not multiple-testing-adjusted.

charts.alt:
The baseline changes the donor-ideology answer. 2026 House Democrats: a 0.5-point more conservative donor score. The lower two rows use exactly the same
candidates, isolating the benchmark change. The full-sample to restricted-sample change mixes attrition and specification, whereas the lower two rows isolate presidential benchmark choice on identical IDs. The 2020 benchmark is allowed only on independently qualified election maps. This sensitivity argues against treating a single positive coefficient as a universal moderation premium or Split Ticket WAR.

charts.alt:
Same candidates, different ideology signals. 2026 House: the same 100 Democratic incumbents in 30 states. Separate models versus jointly adjusting
for both measures, with the same lean controls. An audit-added, exploratory comparison, not a prespecified confirmation. The common sample contains only verified Democratic incumbents with both scores; it is not representative of all nominees. All four models use identical candidate IDs, lean/lean-squared and available Republican-incumbency controls. Donor ideology describes historical funding coalitions; Nokken-Poole measures recorded congressional votes. Their different scales and opposing associations prohibit a single moderate/progressive ranking. Intervals are pointwise, without multiplicity adjustment.

charts.alt:
What the congressional voting record shows. House: ideology uses prior-Congress votes; 2026 party defection uses votes cast before Election Day. The
two measures have different increments. 2026 ideology is the Congress-specific Nokken-Poole first dimension from 2023-2024 votes, not DW-NOMINATE or current campaign positions. The 2026 defection rate uses qualifying recorded votes from January 2025 through November 2, 2026; older years use prior-completed-Congress records. Changing cohorts and timing prevent a formal trend interpretation. Separate increments are not a ranking of the measures. See CSV for exact sample sizes and Holm values.

charts.alt:
House incumbency across six elections. Democratic House incumbents versus nonincumbents, controlling for district lean and Republican
incumbency. 2026 is the primary election. Separate annual chamber-specific lean/lean-squared regressions; the cross-year points are not a paired-candidate or formal trend test. Presidential election years use same-year presidential benchmarks; midterms use lagged benchmarks. Historical cohorts are not the complete 2026 candidate roster. Unknown incumbency is not coded as nonincumbency. These are associations, not causal incumbency effects.

charts.alt:
Caucus membership is a thin test of moderation. Blue Dog minus Progressive Caucus structural residuals. Hollow points are diagnostic: at least one group
falls short of the support gates. Blue Dog/CPC groups are distinct from Blue Dog PAC/CPC PAC endorsements, New Democrats, DSA and Justice Democrats. A 2026 roster of 10 Blue Dogs leaves eight eligible nominees in this model; this does not reconcile the external chart's group of 12. Small membership cohorts, changing benchmark vintages and wide uncertainty do not establish that a moderation premium shrank.

charts.alt:
A complete roster is not complete candidate data. Share of all named 2026 House candidates with usable source information. A missing record does not mean
that a candidate lacks a trait or position. The denominator is 1284 named House candidates across all 435 districts, not one selected Democrat per district or just winners. Aggregate write-in/none-of-the-above choices are retained separately. Background includes historical records, dated office questionnaires and candidate-supplied voter-guide fields, not complete verified biographies. Historical profile headings without extracted facts do not count in this panel. Third-party gaps remain substantial and never mean no experience. Registration-district differences are disclosed; stable FEC IDs can persist across district moves. No machine-extracted trait or newly attached score has been added to the existing performance models.
